statement: The square on the side of a rational plus a medial area applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fifth binomial.
heath_proof: Let AB be the side of a rational plus a medial area, divided into its straight lines at C, so that AC is the greater; let a rational straight line DE be set out, and let there be applied to DE the parallelogram DF equal to the square on AB, producing DG as its breadth; I say that DG is a fifth binomial straight line. Let the same construction as before be made. Since then AB is the side of a rational plus a medial area, divided at C, therefore AC, CB are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, but the rectangle contained by them rational. [X. 40] Since then the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, therefore DL is medial, so that DM is rational and incommensurable in length with DE. [X. 22] Again, since twice the rectangle AC, CB, that is MF, is rational, therefore MG is rational and commensurable with DE. [X. 20] Therefore DM is incommensurable with MG; [X. 13] therefore DM, MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore DG is binomial. [X. 36] I say next that it is also a fifth binomial straight line. For it can be proved similarly that the rectangle DK, KM is equal to the square on MN, and that DK is incommensurable in length with KM; therefore the square on DM is greater than the square on MG by the square on a straight line incommensurable with DM. [X. 18] And DM, MG are commensurable in square only, and the less, MG, is commensurable in length with DE. Therefore DG is a fifth binomial.
ai_proof_text:
10.64
**Statement:** The square on the side of a rational plus a medial area applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fifth binomial.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of a rational plus a medial area, and let it be divided into its terms at C, so that AC is the greater segment. By the definition of this irrational (10.40), AC and CB are straight lines incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial, and the rectangle contained by AC and CB is rational.

**Step 2.** Let DE be a rational straight line. Apply the square on AB to DE, producing as breadth DG, so that the rectangle DE by DG equals the square on AB.

**Step 3.** By 2.4, the square on AB equals the sum of the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB.

**Step 4.** Apply the sum of the squares on AC and CB to DE, producing as breadth DH, so that the rectangle DE by DH equals the sum of the squares on AC and CB. Apply twice the rectangle AC by CB to DE, producing as breadth HG, so that the rectangle DE by HG equals twice the rectangle AC by CB. Then DG equals DH plus HG.

**Step 5.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial and DE is rational, by 10.22 the breadth DH is rational and incommensurable in length with DE.

**Step 6.** Since twice the rectangle AC by CB is rational (for the rectangle AC by CB is rational, so twice it is also rational, being commensurable with it by 10.6) and DE is rational, by 10.20 the breadth HG is rational and commensurable in length with DE.

**Step 7.** Since DH is incommensurable in length with DE and HG is commensurable in length with DE, by 10.13 DH is incommensurable in length with HG.

**Step 8.** Both DH and HG are rational, and they are incommensurable in length with one another. Therefore by 10.36 the whole DG is a binomial straight line.

**Step 9.** We now show that DH is greater than HG. Since AC and CB are incommensurable in square, they are unequal. The square on AC is not equal to the square on CB, so by CN5 the sum of the squares on AC and CB is greater than twice the rectangle AC by CB (for the square on AC plus the square on CB exceeds twice the rectangle AC by CB by the square on the difference, as shown by 2.7). Since these areas are applied to the same line DE, it follows that DH is greater than HG.

**Step 10.** Since the rectangle DE by DH equals the sum of the squares on AC and CB, and the rectangle DE by HG equals twice the rectangle AC by CB, the square on DH is to the square on HG as the square on the sum of squares on AC and CB is to the square on twice the rectangle AC by CB (for each is determined by the ratio of the corresponding areas applied to DE, and by 6.1 areas applied to the same line are as their breadths, so DH is to HG as the sum of the squares on AC, CB is to twice the rectangle AC by CB, and by 6.22 the square on DH is to the square on HG as the square on the sum of the squares on AC, CB is to the square on twice the rectangle AC by CB).

**Step 11.** Now the square on DH minus the square on HG is as the square on the sum of the squares on AC, CB minus the square on twice the rectangle AC by CB, all in ratio to the square on DE. Observe that the square on the sum of the squares on AC, CB minus the square on twice the rectangle AC by CB equals the square on the difference of the squares on AC and CB (by 2.5 applied to the quantities AC squared and CB squared, since (AC² + CB²)² - (2·AC·CB)² = (AC² + CB² + 2·AC·CB)(AC² + CB² - 2·AC·CB) = (AC + CB)²·(AC - CB)² by 2.4 and 2.7, but more directly (AC² + CB²)² - 4·AC²·CB² = (AC² - CB²)²). Therefore the square on DH exceeds the square on HG by a quantity proportional to the square on (AC² - CB²)/DE.

**Step 12.** We must determine whether this excess is commensurable or incommensurable with DH. Now DH is to the excess-line as (AC² + CB²) is to (AC² - CB²). Since AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the squares on AC and CB are incommensurable with one another. By 10.16, the sum AC² + CB² is incommensurable with each of AC² and CB². Likewise AC² + CB² is incommensurable with AC² - CB², for if AC² + CB² were commensurable with AC² - CB², then by 10.15 their sum (which is 2·AC²) and their difference (which is 2·CB²) would be commensurable with each of them, and hence 2·AC² would be commensurable with 2·CB², making AC² commensurable with CB², contradicting that AC and CB are incommensurable in square. Therefore AC² + CB² is incommensurable with AC² - CB², so DH is incommensurable in length with the straight line whose square equals the excess of the square on DH over the square on HG.

**Step 13.** Thus the square on DH (the greater term) exceeds the square on HG (the lesser term) by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DH. Moreover, the lesser term HG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE set out (Step 6), while the greater term DH is not commensurable in length with DE (Step 5).

**Step 14.** By the definition of the fifth binomial (D10.2.5), a binomial straight line where the square on the greater term exceeds the square on the lesser by the square on a line incommensurable with the greater, and where the lesser term is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, is a fifth binomial. Therefore DG is a fifth binomial straight line.

**Step 15.** Therefore the square on the side of a rational plus a medial area, applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth the fifth binomial. Q.E.D.
